    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove the guide named by short_code; with no short_code, nothing is deleted and the user's guides are listed.

short_code.description: Short code of one guide, from an earlier call's result. Required by delete. With check or update, targets that guide instead of the most recently updated one.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.content:
# Why Is the Minipill So Strict?

**Modeling hormone levels in progestin-only and combined birth control pills**

02-120 Programming for Scientists · Fall 2026 · Final Project

> **Status:** In progress. The first version of the app goes live by November 20.
>
> **Live app:** _link coming_ · **Video demo:** _link coming_

> This is an educational model built for a course project. It is not medical advice. If you have questions about your own birth control, talk to a doctor or pharmacist.

---

## The question

The progestin-only "minipill" has to be taken within a 3-hour window: CDC guidance counts a minipill taken more than 3 hours late as missed. A single combined pill, on the other hand, can be up to 48 hours late without needing backup contraception.

**Why the difference?** This project tests how much of it comes down to how fast each hormone leaves the body (its half-life), and how much comes from the two hormones in the combined pill affecting each other.

My starting hypothesis:

- **Norethindrone**, the hormone in the minipill, has a half-life of about 8 hours, so very little is left by the time the next pill is due.
- **Levonorgestrel**, the progestin in the combined pill, lasts about 30 to 36 hours.
- The **estrogen** in the combined pill (ethinyl estradiol) makes the liver produce more SHBG, a blood protein that binds levonorgestrel and slows its clearance. So levonorgestrel builds up over the month in a way norethindrone never does.

## What the program does

The app simulates hormone levels in the blood over a full pill pack, with both pills side by side. You can:

- choose a pill: the minipill (0.35 mg norethindrone) or a combined pill (levonorgestrel + ethinyl estradiol, 21 active / 7 placebo);
- take each dose on time, late, or not at all;
- watch how far hormone levels fall and how long they take to recover.

There is no single "safe" hormone level, because the minipill only stops ovulation in about half of users and works largely by thickening cervical mucus. So instead of using a made-up threshold, the app compares each pill against itself: **how far below that pill's usual daily low point do levels fall when a dose is 3 hours late versus 48 hours late?** If the drops are similar, half-life explains the timing rules. If not, something else must matter too.

## How the model works

Each hormone uses a compartment model with oral absorption. A pill puts a dose into the gut, the hormone moves from the gut into the blood, and the body clears it from the blood:

$$\frac{dG}{dt} = -k_a G$$

$$\frac{dC}{dt} = \frac{F \, k_a \, G}{V} - k \, C, \qquad k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| G | amount of hormone still in the gut |
| C | concentration of hormone in the blood |
| kₐ | absorption rate (chosen to match each drug's time to peak) |
| F | fraction of the dose that reaches the blood (bioavailability) |
| V | volume of distribution |
| k | elimination rate, set by the half-life |

Each pill taken adds one dose to G at the time it's taken.

**Second compartment (norethindrone).** The one-compartment model can't match norethindrone's measured levels (see checks below), so norethindrone gets a second, "tissue" compartment that exchanges drug with the blood:

$$\frac{dA_1}{dt} = F \, k_a \, G - (k_{10} + k_{12}) A_1 + k_{21} A_2, \qquad \frac{dA_2}{dt} = k_{12} A_1 - k_{21} A_2, \qquad C = \frac{A_1}{V_1}$$

After a dose, levels first fall quickly as drug moves into the tissues (half-life ≈ 0.8 h), then slowly as it is eliminated (half-life ≈ 7.8 h). The five rates and volume are **fitted** to the label's single-dose values (time to peak, peak, average and 24-hour levels, half-life) by `scripts/fit_norethindrone.py`, not measured. The fit can't separate absorption from the fast tissue phase, so those two rates individually aren't well determined; the curve itself is.

**Planned additions:**

- **The estrogen–SHBG effect:** ethinyl estradiol slowly raises SHBG over the cycle, and higher SHBG slows levonorgestrel clearance. The strength and speed of this effect aren't reported directly, so I calibrate them to match published data and say so clearly.

## How I know it's right

| Check | What it tests | Expected result | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exact single-dose solution | The numerical simulation | Matches the Bateman function (one compartment) and the exact matrix solution (two compartments) | ✅ Passing |
| Mass balance | No drug appears or disappears | Absorbed + eliminated + remaining = total dose | ✅ Passing |
| Steady-state accumulation | Repeated daily dosing | 1 / (1 − e^(−kτ)): ≈ 1.14 for norethindrone, ≈ 2.35 for levonorgestrel (30 h half-life) | ✅ Passing |
| Norethindrone single dose | Published label values | Peak ≈ 4,800 pg/mL near 1.2 h; ≈ 130 pg/mL at 24 h | ❌ One compartment (7.6-fold drop vs. 37-fold) · ✅ Two compartments (all label values within 5%) |
| Combined pill steady state | Published label values (0.10 mg levonorgestrel) | Steady state from day 19; peak ≈ 6.0 ng/mL, low ≈ 1.9 ng/mL | ☐ Planned |
| SHBG effect | A behavior the science requires | Without SHBG, the model underpredicts levonorgestrel's 3- to 4-fold rise; with it, the gap closes | ☐ Planned |

As expected, the one-compartment model **fails** the norethindrone 24-hour check: the measured drop is about 37-fold in 24 hours, much steeper than the 7.6-fold an 8-hour half-life predicts. A second compartment fixes it: the steep early drop is drug moving into the tissues, not leaving the body.

| Norethindrone, single 0.35 mg dose | Label | One compartment | Two compartments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time to peak | 1.2 ± 0.5 h | 1.2 h | 1.18 h |
| Peak | 4,817 ± 1,533 pg/mL | 851 pg/mL | 4,724 pg/mL |
| Average over 24 h | 885 ± 250 pg/mL | — | 914 pg/mL |
| Level at 24 h | 130 ± 47 pg/mL | 113 pg/mL | 129 pg/mL |
| Half-life | 7.7 ± 0.5 h | 7.7 h (input) | 7.8 h |

The fitted model implies a clearance of about 230 L/day and a volume of about 1 L/kg, lower than the label's "about 600 L/day" and "about 4 L/kg". Those label figures come from separate studies and don't match the label's own concentration data, so I fit to the concentrations.

## Running it

**Online:** Use the live app (link above). Nothing to install.

**Locally** (Python 3.13+):

```
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate        # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**Running the tests:**

```
pytest
```

**Refitting norethindrone** (prints the fitted values to copy into `src/minipill/params.py`):

```
python scripts/fit_norethindrone.py
```

## Repository layout

```
sources/    Drug labels and papers the parameters come from
src/        The model and simulation code
tests/      Checks against exact solutions and published values
scripts/    Parameter fitting
app/        The web app (norethindrone_preview.html: early interactive charts)
journal/    Claude Code session logs (my build journal)
```

_This layout will be updated as the project grows._

## Key parameters

Full tables, with sources for every value, are in [`sources/`](sources/).

| Hormone | Half-life | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Norethindrone (minipill) | 7.7 ± 0.5 h | Peak ≈ 1.2 h after a dose; taken daily with no break |
| Levonorgestrel (combined) | ≈ 30 h single dose; 36 ± 13 h at steady state | Binds SHBG; rises 3- to 4-fold over the cycle |
| Ethinyl estradiol (combined) | ≈ 15 h single dose; 18 ± 4.7 h at steady state | Raises SHBG ≈ 1.7-fold; broken down partly by CYP3A4 |

## Assumptions and limitations

- Hormone level is used as a stand-in for protection. In reality, the minipill also works through cervical mucus, and the model doesn't simulate ovulation itself.
- Parameters are averages from label studies. Real people vary, and published data show that body weight can roughly double levonorgestrel's half-life.
- The SHBG effect is calibrated to match published data, not measured directly.
- Drug interactions, food, and vomiting or diarrhea are not modeled (yet).

## Possible extensions

- **Body weight:** reproduce published differences in levonorgestrel kinetics between normal-BMI and obese users (Edelman et al., 2009), then see what the model predicts for the minipill, where no such data exist.
- **Drug interactions:** a drug like rifampin speeds up the enzyme that breaks down ethinyl estradiol, which should lower SHBG and then levonorgestrel.

## Sources

- Teorell, T. (1937). Kinetics of distribution of substances administered to the body. *Archives Internationales de Pharmacodynamie et de Thérapie*, 57.

The search turned up the CDC flowchart for late or missed combined oral contraceptives, which is part of the 2024 U.S. SPR. I did not open the full PDF, so these points come from search snippets.

- **Pill less than 24 hours late:** The guidance is to take the pill right away and keep the rest at the usual time. Take the late or missed pill as soon as possible. Continue taking the remaining pills at the usual time (even if it means taking two pills on the same day). No additional contraceptive protection is needed.
- **One pill 24 to under 48 hours missed:** The snippet is fragmentary, but it indicates that backup contraception is not usually needed but can be considered (with the exception of UPA) if hormonal pills were missed earlier in the cycle or in the last week of the previous cycle.
- **Two or more consecutive pills missed (48 hours or more):** Take the most recent missed pill as soon as possible (any other missed pills should be discarded). Continue taking the remaining pills at the usual time (even if it means taking two pills on the same day). Use back-up contraception (e.g., condoms) or avoid sexual intercourse until hormonal pills have been taken for 7 consecutive days.
- **Pills missed in the last week of the pack:** Omit the hormone-free interval by finishing the hormonal pills in the current pack and starting a new pack the next day.

Sources and currency: The CDC's own PDF is titled "Recommended Actions After Late or Missed Combined Oral Contraceptives," and the CDC Stacks record lists its publication date as 2024/08/14. A Contraceptive Technology copy of the same flowchart is also available. One caveat: The Skimm notes that the 2024 guidance was the US government's guidance prior to that date and time and does not reflect the guidance of the current or subsequent administrations. I did not confirm whether the CDC has changed or removed these recommendations since then, so check the CDC SPR page before relying on them.

# Why Is the Minipill So Strict?

**Modeling hormone levels in progestin-only and combined birth control pills**

02-120 Programming for Scientists · Fall 2026 · Final Project

> **Status:** In progress. The first version of the app goes live by November 20.
>
> **Live app:** _link coming_ · **Video demo:** _link coming_

> This is an educational model built for a course project. It is not medical advice. If you have questions about your own birth control, talk to a doctor or pharmacist.

---

## The question

The progestin-only "minipill" has to be taken within a 3-hour window: CDC guidance counts a minipill taken more than 3 hours late as missed. A single combined pill, on the other hand, can be up to 48 hours late without needing backup contraception.

**Why the difference?** This project tests how much of it comes down to how fast each hormone leaves the body (its half-life), and how much comes from the two hormones in the combined pill affecting each other.

My starting hypothesis:

- **Norethindrone**, the hormone in the minipill, has a half-life of about 8 hours, so very little is left by the time the next pill is due.
- **Levonorgestrel**, the progestin in the combined pill, lasts about 30 to 36 hours.
- The **estrogen** in the combined pill (ethinyl estradiol) makes the liver produce more SHBG, a blood protein that binds levonorgestrel and slows its clearance. So levonorgestrel builds up over the month in a way norethindrone never does.

## What the program does

The app simulates hormone levels in the blood over a full pill pack, with both pills side by side. You can:

- choose a pill: the minipill (0.35 mg norethindrone) or a combined pill (levonorgestrel + ethinyl estradiol, 21 active / 7 placebo);
- take each dose on time, late, or not at all;
- watch how far hormone levels fall and how long they take to recover.

There is no single "safe" hormone level, because the minipill only stops ovulation in about half of users and works largely by thickening cervical mucus. So instead of using a made-up threshold, the app compares each pill against itself: **how far below that pill's usual daily low point do levels fall when a dose is 3 hours late versus 48 hours late?** If the drops are similar, half-life explains the timing rules. If not, something else must matter too.

## How the model works

Each hormone uses a compartment model with oral absorption. A pill puts a dose into the gut, the hormone moves from the gut into the blood, and the body clears it from the blood:

$$\frac{dG}{dt} = -k_a G$$

$$\frac{dC}{dt} = \frac{F \, k_a \, G}{V} - k \, C, \qquad k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| G | amount of hormone still in the gut |
| C | concentration of hormone in the blood |
| kₐ | absorption rate (chosen to match each drug's time to peak) |
| F | fraction of the dose that reaches the blood (bioavailability) |
| V | volume of distribution |
| k | elimination rate, set by the half-life |

Each pill taken adds one dose to G at the time it's taken.

**Second compartment (norethindrone).** The one-compartment model can't match norethindrone's measured levels (see checks below), so norethindrone gets a second, "tissue" compartment that exchanges drug with the blood:

$$\frac{dA_1}{dt} = F \, k_a \, G - (k_{10} + k_{12}) A_1 + k_{21} A_2, \qquad \frac{dA_2}{dt} = k_{12} A_1 - k_{21} A_2, \qquad C = \frac{A_1}{V_1}$$

After a dose, levels first fall quickly as drug moves into the tissues (half-life ≈ 0.8 h), then slowly as it is eliminated (half-life ≈ 7.8 h). The five rates and volume are **fitted** to the label's single-dose values (time to peak, peak, average and 24-hour levels, half-life) by `scripts/fit_norethindrone.py`, not measured. The fit can't separate absorption from the fast tissue phase, so those two rates individually aren't well determined; the curve itself is.

**Planned additions:**

- **The estrogen–SHBG effect:** ethinyl estradiol slowly raises SHBG over the cycle, and higher SHBG slows levonorgestrel clearance. The strength and speed of this effect aren't reported directly, so I calibrate them to match published data and say so clearly.

## How I know it's right

| Check | What it tests | Expected result | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exact single-dose solution | The numerical simulation | Matches the Bateman function (one compartment) and the exact matrix solution (two compartments) | ✅ Passing |
| Mass balance | No drug appears or disappears | Absorbed + eliminated + remaining = total dose | ✅ Passing |
| Steady-state accumulation | Repeated daily dosing | 1 / (1 − e^(−kτ)): ≈ 1.14 for norethindrone, ≈ 2.35 for levonorgestrel (30 h half-life) | ✅ Passing |
| Norethindrone single dose | Published label values | Peak ≈ 4,800 pg/mL near 1.2 h; ≈ 130 pg/mL at 24 h | ❌ One compartment (7.6-fold drop vs. 37-fold) · ✅ Two compartments (all label values within 5%) |
| Combined pill steady state | Published label values (0.10 mg levonorgestrel) | Steady state from day 19; peak ≈ 6.0 ng/mL, low ≈ 1.9 ng/mL | ☐ Planned |
| SHBG effect | A behavior the science requires | Without SHBG, the model underpredicts levonorgestrel's 3- to 4-fold rise; with it, the gap closes | ☐ Planned |

As expected, the one-compartment model **fails** the norethindrone 24-hour check: the measured drop is about 37-fold in 24 hours, much steeper than the 7.6-fold an 8-hour half-life predicts. A second compartment fixes it: the steep early drop is drug moving into the tissues, not leaving the body.

| Norethindrone, single 0.35 mg dose | Label | One compartment | Two compartments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time to peak | 1.2 ± 0.5 h | 1.2 h | 1.18 h |
| Peak | 4,817 ± 1,533 pg/mL | 851 pg/mL | 4,724 pg/mL |
| Average over 24 h | 885 ± 250 pg/mL | — | 914 pg/mL |
| Level at 24 h | 130 ± 47 pg/mL | 113 pg/mL | 129 pg/mL |
| Half-life | 7.7 ± 0.5 h | 7.7 h (input) | 7.8 h |

The fitted model implies a clearance of about 230 L/day and a volume of about 1 L/kg, lower than the label's "about 600 L/day" and "about 4 L/kg". Those label figures come from separate studies and don't match the label's own concentration data, so I fit to the concentrations.

## Running it

**Online:** Use the live app (link above). Nothing to install.

**Locally** (Python 3.13+):

```
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate        # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**Running the tests:**

```
pytest
```

**Refitting norethindrone** (prints the fitted values to copy into `src/minipill/params.py`):

```
python scripts/fit_norethindrone.py
```

## Repository layout

```
sources/    Drug labels and papers the parameters come from
src/        The model and simulation code
tests/      Checks against exact solutions and published values
scripts/    Parameter fitting
app/        The web app (norethindrone_preview.html: early interactive charts)
journal/    Claude Code session logs (my build journal)
```

_This layout will be updated as the project grows._

## Key parameters

Full tables, with sources for every value, are in [`sources/`](sources/).

| Hormone | Half-life | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Norethindrone (minipill) | 7.7 ± 0.5 h | Peak ≈ 1.2 h after a dose; taken daily with no break |
| Levonorgestrel (combined) | ≈ 30 h single dose; 36 ± 13 h at steady state | Binds SHBG; rises 3- to 4-fold over the cycle |
| Ethinyl estradiol (combined) | ≈ 15 h single dose; 18 ± 4.7 h at steady state | Raises SHBG ≈ 1.7-fold; broken down partly by CYP3A4 |

## Assumptions and limitations

- Hormone level is used as a stand-in for protection. In reality, the minipill also works through cervical mucus, and the model doesn't simulate ovulation itself.
- Parameters are averages from label studies. Real people vary, and published data show that body weight can roughly double levonorgestrel's half-life.
- The SHBG effect is calibrated to match published data, not measured directly.
- Drug interactions, food, and vomiting or diarrhea are not modeled (yet).

## Possible extensions

- **Body weight:** reproduce published differences in levonorgestrel kinetics between normal-BMI and obese users (Edelman et al., 2009), then see what the model predicts for the minipill, where no such data exist.
- **Drug interactions:** a drug like rifampin speeds up the enzyme that breaks down ethinyl estradiol, which should lower SHBG and then levonorgestrel.

## Sources

- Teorell, T. (1937). Kinetics of distribution of substances administered to the body. *Archives Internationales de Pharmacodynamie et de Thérapie*, 57.
- [Norethindrone 0.35 mg prescribing information](https://medlibrary.org/lib/rx/meds/norethindrone/)
- [Levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol prescribing information (Alesse)](https://www.drugs.com/pro/alesse.html)
- [Levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol prescribing information (Seasonale)](https://www.drugs.com/pro/seasonale.html)
- [Levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol package insert (Levette)](https://www.sahpra.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Levette_PI_Actor-Pharma_MCC-FormatJuly-2015.pdf)
- [CDC recommended actions after late or missed pills (UCSF summary)](https://beyondthepill.ucsf.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/recommended-action-late-missed-progestin-508.pdf)
- Edelman, A. B., et al. (2009). [Impact of obesity on oral contraceptive pharmacokinetics and hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian activity](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2736633). *Contraception*, 80(2), 119–127.

content.content:
## The question

The progestin-only "minipill" has to be taken within a 3-hour window: CDC guidance counts a minipill taken more than 3 hours late as missed [1]. A single combined pill, on the other hand, can be up to 48 hours late without needing backup contraception; only at 48 hours or more (two or more pills missed) does the CDC advise condoms or abstinence until 7 days of pills have been taken in a row [2].

> **[1]** CDC. *Recommended Actions After Late or Missed Progestin-Only Pills* (CS39620-D). U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024. [`sources/cdc_missedpill_guidance.pdf`](sources/cdc_missedpill_guidance.pdf) ([copy hosted by UCSF Beyond the Pill](https://beyondthepill.ucsf.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/recommended-action-late-missed-progestin-508.pdf))
>
> **[2]** CDC. *Recommended Actions After Late or Missed Combined Oral Contraceptives* (CS39620-C). U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024. [doi:10.15620/cdc/251909](https://doi.org/10.15620/cdc/251909) · [`sources/cdc_missedpill_combined.pdf`](sources/cdc_missedpill_combined.pdf)

**Why the difference?** This project tests how much of it comes down to how fast each hormone leaves the body (its half-life), and how much comes from the two hormones in the combined pill affecting each other.

"""Drug parameters, with sources. See sources/Model Parameters .pdf for the full table."""

from minipill.pk import Drug, ka_from_tmax

# Assumed body weight to turn the label's L/kg volume into litres. Not from a source.
BODY_WEIGHT_KG = 60.0

# --- Norethindrone (minipill) ------------------------------------------------
NORETHINDRONE_DOSE_MG = 0.35  # taken every 24 h, no break

# Label values to check the model against (norethindrone label, single 0.35 mg dose).
NORETHINDRONE_LABEL = {
    "tmax_h": 1.2,  # ± 0.5
    "cmax_pg_ml": 4817,  # ± 1533
    "cavg_24h_pg_ml": 885,  # ± 250
    "c24_pg_ml": 130,  # ± 47
    "half_life_h": 7.7,  # ± 0.5
}

# Two-compartment model (the one to use).
# F is from the label (absolute bioavailability ≈ 65%). The other five values are
# FITTED by scripts/fit_norethindrone.py to the five label values above; they are
# not measured. The fit reproduces every label value within 3%.
#
# Notes on the fit:
#  - Any starting point gives the same fit, always with ka ≈ alpha (the fast
#    distribution rate, ≈ 0.91 /h). The label's summary values can't tell absorption
#    and distribution apart, so ka and alpha individually are not well determined;
#    the curve shape, 24 h level and terminal phase are.
#  - Implied clearance ≈ 234 L/day and Vss ≈ 57 L (≈ 1 L/kg at 60 kg), lower than the
#    label's ~600 L/day and ~4 L/kg. Those label figures come from different studies
#    and don't match the label's own concentration data.
NORETHINDRONE = Drug(
    name="norethindrone",
    ka=0.911,  # 1/h, fitted
    F=0.65,  # norethindrone label
    V_L=18.7,  # L, central volume, fitted
    k10=0.520,  # 1/h, fitted
    k12=0.320,  # 1/h, fitted
    k21=0.155,  # 1/h, fitted
)

# One-compartment model, kept for comparison: it gives a ~8-fold drop from peak to
# 24 h instead of the label's ~37-fold, and with the label's 4 L/kg volume it
# underpredicts the peak about 5-fold.
NORETHINDRONE_1C = Drug.one_compartment(
    name="norethindrone (1 compartment)",
    half_life_h=7.7,  # norethindrone label
    ka=ka_from_tmax(1.2, 7.7),  # ESTIMATED: chosen so Tmax = 1.2 h (label); ≈ 3.0 /h
    F=0.65,  # norethindrone label
    V_L=4.0 * BODY_WEIGHT_KG,  # norethindrone label, ≈ 4 L/kg
)
"""Compartment pharmacokinetic model with first-order oral absorption.

One or two compartments: with k12 = k21 = 0 the peripheral compartment is
never reached and this is the one-compartment model.

Units used throughout: time in hours, amounts in mg, volume in L,
so concentrations come out in mg/L (use ``mg_per_l_to_pg_per_ml`` to compare
with drug-label values).

State variables (all amounts, in mg):
    gut          drug still waiting to be absorbed            G
    central      drug in the blood                            A1  (C = A1 / V)
    peripheral   drug that has moved into the tissues         A2
    eliminated   drug cleared from the blood                  E
    first_pass   drug lost before reaching the blood (1 - F)  L

    dG/dt  = -ka G
    dA1/dt =  F ka G - (k10 + k12) A1 + k21 A2
    dA2/dt =  k12 A1 - k21 A2
    dE/dt  =  k10 A1
    dL/dt  = (1 - F) ka G

Tracking E and L as well as G, A1 and A2 means their sum always equals the
total dose taken, which gives an exact mass-balance check on the numerical solver.
"""

from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.optimize import brentq

LN2 = np.log(2)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Drug:
    """Parameters for one hormone."""

    name: str
    ka: float  # absorption rate constant, 1/h
    F: float  # oral bioavailability, 0-1
    V_L: float  # volume of the central (blood) compartment, L
    k10: float  # elimination rate from the central compartment, 1/h
    k12: float = 0.0  # central -> peripheral, 1/h
    k21: float = 0.0  # peripheral -> central, 1/h

    def __post_init__(self):
        if min(self.ka, self.F, self.V_L, self.k10) <= 0 or self.F > 1:
            raise ValueError("ka, V_L, k10 must be > 0 and 0 < F <= 1")
        if self.k12 < 0 or self.k21 < 0 or (self.k12 > 0) != (self.k21 > 0):
            raise ValueError("k12 and k21 must both be 0 (one compartment) or both > 0")

    @classmethod
    def one_compartment(cls, name, half_life_h, ka, F, V_L):
        return cls(name=name, ka=ka, F=F, V_L=V_L, k10=LN2 / half_life_h)

    @property
    def n_compartments(self) -> int:
        return 2 if self.k12 > 0 else 1

    @property
    def disposition_rates(self) -> tuple[float, ...]:
        """Rates of the exponential phases after absorption: (k10,) or (alpha, beta), alpha > beta."""
        if self.n_compartments == 1:
            return (self.k10,)
        s = self.k10 + self.k12 + self.k21
        root = np.sqrt(s * s - 4 * self.k10 * self.k21)
        return ((s + root) / 2, (s - root) / 2)

    @property
    def terminal_rate(self) -> float:
        """Slowest elimination rate, 1/h (sets the terminal half-life)."""
        return self.disposition_rates[-1]

    @property
    def terminal_half_life_h(self) -> float:
        return LN2 / self.terminal_rate

    @property
    def clearance_L_per_h(self) -> float:
        return self.k10 * self.V_L

    @property
    def vss_L(self) -> float:
        """Volume of distribution at steady state, V1 (1 + k12 / k21)."""
        return self.V_L * (1 + self.k12 / self.k21) if self.k12 > 0 else self.V_L


@dataclass
class SimResult:
    t: np.ndarray  # h
    gut: np.ndarray  # mg
    central: np.ndarray  # mg
    peripheral: np.ndarray  # mg
    eliminated: np.ndarray  # mg
    first_pass: np.ndarray  # mg
    conc: np.ndarray  # mg/L
    dosed: np.ndarray  # mg taken so far at each time point


def mg_per_l_to_pg_per_ml(c):
    """1 mg/L = 1e9 pg / 1e3 mL = 1e6 pg/mL."""
    return np.asarray(c) * 1e6


def mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(c):
    """1 mg/L = 1e3 ng/mL."""
    return np.asarray(c) * 1e3


def _rhs(t, y, ka, F, k10, k12, k21):
    G, A1, A2, _E, _L = y
    absorbed = ka * G
    return [
        -absorbed,
        F * absorbed - (k10 + k12) * A1 + k21 * A2,
        k12 * A1 - k21 * A2,
        k10 * A1,
        (1 - F) * absorbed,
    ]


def simulate(drug: Drug, dose_times, dose_mg: float, t_eval, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-14) -> SimResult:
    """Simulate blood levels for a list of pill times.

    Each pill adds ``dose_mg`` to the gut at its time. Late or missed pills are
    just different ``dose_times``. Two pills at the same time count as a double dose.

    Pills at or after the last time in ``t_eval`` are not simulated.
    """
    t_eval = np.asarray(t_eval, dtype=float)
    if t_eval.ndim != 1 or len(t_eval) == 0:
        raise ValueError("t_eval must be a non-empty 1-D array")
    if np.any(np.diff(t_eval) <= 0) or t_eval[0] < 0:
        raise ValueError("t_eval must be increasing and start at or after 0")
    dose_times = [float(d) for d in dose_times]
    if any(d < 0 for d in dose_times):
        raise ValueError("dose times must be >= 0")

    t_start, t_end = 0.0, t_eval[-1]
    doses_at = Counter(d for d in dose_times if d < t_end)
    breakpoints = sorted({t_start, t_end, *doses_at})
    args = (drug.ka, drug.F, drug.k10, drug.k12, drug.k21)

    y = np.zeros(5)
    total_dosed = 0.0
    out = np.full((5, len(t_eval)), np.nan)
    dosed = np.zeros(len(t_eval))

    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(breakpoints[:-1], breakpoints[1:])):
        n = doses_at.get(a, 0)
        y[0] += n * dose_mg
        total_dosed += n * dose_mg

        last = i == len(breakpoints) - 2
        mask = (t_eval >= a) & ((t_eval <= b) if last else (t_eval < b))
        pts = np.unique(np.concatenate([t_eval[mask], [a, b]]))
        sol = solve_ivp(_rhs, (a, b), y, t_eval=pts, args=args, method="LSODA", rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
        if not sol.success:
            raise RuntimeError(f"ODE solver failed on [{a}, {b}]: {sol.message}")

        idx = np.searchsorted(pts, t_eval[mask])
        out[:, mask] = sol.y[:, idx]
        dosed[mask] = total_dosed
        y = sol.y[:, -1].copy()

    gut, central, peripheral, eliminated, first_pass = out
    return SimResult(
        t=t_eval, gut=gut, central=central, peripheral=peripheral, eliminated=eliminated,
        first_pass=first_pass, conc=central / drug.V_L, dosed=dosed,
    )


def bateman(drug: Drug, dose_mg: float, t):
    """Exact one-compartment concentration (mg/L) after one dose at t = 0 (needs ka != k10)."""
    if drug.n_compartments != 1:
        raise ValueError("bateman() is for one-compartment drugs; use exact_single_dose()")
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    ka, k = drug.ka, drug.k10
    if np.isclose(ka, k):
        raise ValueError("Bateman formula needs ka != k10")
    c = drug.F * dose_mg * ka / (drug.V_L * (ka - k)) * (np.exp(-k * t) - np.exp(-ka * t))
    return np.where(t >= 0, c, 0.0)


def exact_single_dose(drug: Drug, dose_mg: float, t):
    """Exact concentration (mg/L) after one dose at t = 0, for one or two compartments.

    The model is linear, y' = M y, so y(t) = P exp(D t) P^-1 y0 using the
    eigendecomposition of M. Independent of the ODE solver used in ``simulate``.
    """
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    ka, F, k10, k12, k21 = drug.ka, drug.F, drug.k10, drug.k12, drug.k21
    M = np.array([
        [-ka, 0.0, 0.0],
        [F * ka, -(k10 + k12), k21],
        [0.0, k12, -k21],
    ])
    lam, P = np.linalg.eig(M)
    if np.min(np.abs(np.subtract.outer(lam, lam)) + np.eye(3)) < 1e-9:
        raise ValueError("repeated rates: exact solution needs distinct ka, alpha, beta")
    coef = np.linalg.solve(P, [dose_mg, 0.0, 0.0])
    tt = np.clip(t, 0, None).ravel()
    central = ((P[1] * coef) @ np.exp(np.outer(lam, tt))).reshape(t.shape)
    return np.where(t >= 0, np.real(central) / drug.V_L, 0.0)


def tmax(ka: float, k: float) -> float:
    """One-compartment time of peak concentration after one dose."""
    return np.log(ka / k) / (ka - k)


def ka_from_tmax(tmax_h: float, half_life_h: float) -> float:
    """One-compartment absorption rate that puts the single-dose peak at ``tmax_h``.

    Picks the solution with ka > k (absorption faster than elimination), which
    is the case for every drug in this project.
    """
    k = LN2 / half_life_h
    if tmax_h >= 1 / k:
        raise ValueError(f"tmax must be < 1/k = {1 / k:.2f} h for ka > k")
    return brentq(lambda ka: tmax(ka, k) - tmax_h, k * (1 + 1e-9), 1e4)


def accumulation_ratio(drug: Drug, tau_h: float) -> float:
    """Steady-state / first-dose ratio for doses every ``tau_h`` hours, 1 / (1 - e^(-k tau)).

    Exact for one compartment (k = k10). For two compartments, uses the terminal
    rate, which is approximate.
    """
    return 1 / (1 - np.exp(-drug.terminal_rate * tau_h))
"""Pharmacokinetic model of progestin-only and combined birth control pills."""

    """Parameters for one hormone."""

    name: str
    ka: float  # absorption rate constant, 1/h
    F: float  # oral bioavailability, 0-1
    V_L: float  # volume of the central (blood) compartment, L
    k10: float  # elimination rate from the central compartment, 1/h
    k12: float = 0.0  # central -> peripheral, 1/h
    k21: float = 0.0  # peripheral -> central, 1/h

    def __post_init__(self):
        if min(self.ka, self.F, self.V_L, self.k10) <= 0 or self.F > 1:
            raise ValueError("ka, V_L, k10 must be > 0 and 0 < F <= 1")
        if self.k12 < 0 or self.k21 < 0 or (self.k12 > 0) != (self.k21 > 0):
            raise ValueError("k12 and k21 must both be 0 (one compartment) or both > 0")

    @classmethod
    def one_compartment(cls, name, half_life_h, ka, F, V_L):
        return cls(name=name, ka=ka, F=F, V_L=V_L, k10=LN2 / half_life_h)

    @property
    def n_compartments(self) -> int:
        return 2 if self.k12 > 0 else 1

    @property
    def disposition_rates(self) -> tuple[float, ...]:
        """Rates of the exponential phases after absorption: (k10,) or (alpha, beta), alpha > beta."""
        if self.n_compartments == 1:
            return (self.k10,)
        s = self.k10 + self.k12 + self.k21
        root = np.sqrt(s * s - 4 * self.k10 * self.k21)
        return ((s + root) / 2, (s - root) / 2)

    @property
    def terminal_rate(self) -> float:
        """Slowest elimination rate, 1/h (sets the terminal half-life)."""
        return self.disposition_rates[-1]

    @property
    def terminal_half_life_h(self) -> float:
        return LN2 / self.terminal_rate

    @property
    def clearance_L_per_h(self) -> float:
        return self.k10 * self.V_L

    @property
    def vss_L(self) -> float:
        """Volume of distribution at steady state, V1 (1 + k12 / k21)."""
        return self.V_L * (1 + self.k12 / self.k21) if self.k12 > 0 else self.V_L


@dataclass
class SimResult:
    t: np.ndarray  # h
    gut: np.ndarray  # mg
    central: np.ndarray  # mg
    peripheral: np.ndarray  # mg
    eliminated: np.ndarray  # mg
    first_pass: np.ndarray  # mg
    conc: np.ndarray  # mg/L
    dosed: np.ndarray  # mg taken so far at each time point


def mg_per_l_to_pg_per_ml(c):
    """1 mg/L = 1e9 pg / 1e3 mL = 1e6 pg/mL."""
    return np.asarray(c) * 1e6


def mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(c):
    """1 mg/L = 1e3 ng/mL."""
    return np.asarray(c) * 1e3


def _rhs(t, y, ka, F, k10, k12, k21):
    G, A1, A2, _E, _L = y
    absorbed = ka * G
    return [
        -absorbed,
        F * absorbed - (k10 + k12) * A1 + k21 * A2,
        k12 * A1 - k21 * A2,
        k10 * A1,
        (1 - F) * absorbed,
    ]


def simulate(drug: Drug, dose_times, dose_mg: float, t_eval, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-14) -> SimResult:
    """Simulate blood levels for a list of pill times.

    Each pill adds ``dose_mg`` to the gut at its time. Late or missed pills are
    just different ``dose_times``. Two pills at the same time count as a double dose.

    Pills at or after the last time in ``t_eval`` are not simulated.
    """
    t_eval = np.asarray(t_eval, dtype=float)
    if t_eval.ndim != 1 or len(t_eval) == 0:
        raise ValueError("t_eval must be a non-empty 1-D array")
    if np.any(np.diff(t_eval) <= 0) or t_eval[0] < 0:
        raise ValueError("t_eval must be increasing and start at or after 0")
    dose_times = [float(d) for d in dose_times]
    if any(d < 0 for d in dose_times):
        raise ValueError("dose times must be >= 0")

    t_start, t_end = 0.0, t_eval[-1]
    doses_at = Counter(d for d in dose_times if d < t_end)
    breakpoints = sorted({t_start, t_end, *doses_at})
    args = (drug.ka, drug.F, drug.k10, drug.k12, drug.k21)

    y = np.zeros(5)
    total_dosed = 0.0
    out = np.full((5, len(t_eval)), np.nan)
    dosed = np.zeros(len(t_eval))

    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(breakpoints[:-1], breakpoints[1:])):
        n = doses_at.get(a, 0)
        y[0] += n * dose_mg
        total_dosed += n * dose_mg

        last = i == len(breakpoints) - 2
        mask = (t_eval >= a) & ((t_eval <= b) if last else (t_eval < b))
        pts = np.unique(np.concatenate([t_eval[mask], [a, b]]))
        sol = solve_ivp(_rhs, (a, b), y, t_eval=pts, args=args, method="LSODA", rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
        if not sol.success:
            raise RuntimeError(f"ODE solver failed on [{a}, {b}]: {sol.message}")

        idx = np.searchsorted(pts, t_eval[mask])
        out[:, mask] = sol.y[:, idx]
        dosed[mask] = total_dosed
        y = sol.y[:, -1].copy()

    gut, central, peripheral, eliminated, first_pass = out
    return SimResult(
        t=t_eval, gut=gut, central=central, peripheral=peripheral, eliminated=eliminated,
        first_pass=first_pass, conc=central / drug.V_L, dosed=dosed,
    )


def bateman(drug: Drug, dose_mg: float, t):
    """Exact one-compartment concentration (mg/L) after one dose at t = 0 (needs ka != k10)."""
    if drug.n_compartments != 1:
        raise ValueError("bateman() is for one-compartment drugs; use exact_single_dose()")
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    ka, k = drug.ka, drug.k10
    if np.isclose(ka, k):
        raise ValueError("Bateman formula needs ka != k10")
    c = drug.F * dose_mg * ka / (drug.V_L * (ka - k)) * (np.exp(-k * t) - np.exp(-ka * t))
    return np.where(t >= 0, c, 0.0)


def exact_single_dose(drug: Drug, dose_mg: float, t):
    """Exact concentration (mg/L) after one dose at t = 0, for one or two compartments.

    The model is linear, y' = M y, so y(t) = P exp(D t) P^-1 y0 using the
    eigendecomposition of M. Independent of the ODE solver used in ``simulate``.
    """
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    ka, F, k10, k12, k21 = drug.ka, drug.F, drug.k10, drug.k12, drug.k21
    M = np.array([
        [-ka, 0.0, 0.0],
        [F * ka, -(k10 + k12), k21],
        [0.0, k12, -k21],
    ])
    lam, P = np.linalg.eig(M)
    if np.min(np.abs(np.subtract.outer(lam, lam)) + np.eye(3)) < 1e-9:
        raise ValueError("repeated rates: exact solution needs distinct ka, alpha, beta")
    coef = np.linalg.solve(P, [dose_mg, 0.0, 0.0])
    tt = np.clip(t, 0, None).ravel()
    central = ((P[1] * coef) @ np.exp(np.outer(lam, tt))).reshape(t.shape)
    return np.where(t >= 0, np.real(central) / drug.V_L, 0.0)


def tmax(ka: float, k: float) -> float:
    """One-compartment time of peak concentration after one dose."""
    return np.log(ka / k) / (ka - k)


def ka_from_tmax(tmax_h: float, half_life_h: float) -> float:
    """One-compartment absorption rate that puts the single-dose peak at ``tmax_h``.

    Picks the solution with ka > k (absorption faster than elimination), which
    is the case for every drug in this project.
    """
    k = LN2 / half_life_h
    if tmax_h >= 1 / k:
        raise ValueError(f"tmax must be < 1/k = {1 / k:.2f} h for ka > k")
    return brentq(lambda ka: tmax(ka, k) - tmax_h, k * (1 + 1e-9), 1e4)


def accumulation_ratio(drug: Drug, tau_h: float) -> float:
    """Steady-state / first-dose ratio for doses every ``tau_h`` hours, 1 / (1 - e^(-k tau)).

    Exact for one compartment (k = k10). For two compartments, uses the terminal
    rate, which is approximate.
    """
    return 1 / (1 - np.exp(-drug.terminal_rate * tau_h))

import numpy as np
import pytest

from minipill.params import (
    NORETHINDRONE, NORETHINDRONE_1C, NORETHINDRONE_DOSE_MG, NORETHINDRONE_LABEL,
)
from minipill.pk import (
    Drug, accumulation_ratio, bateman, exact_single_dose, ka_from_tmax, mg_per_l_to_pg_per_ml,
    simulate, tmax,
)

DAY = 24.0
# Generic levonorgestrel-like drug (30 h half-life) for checks that don't need real values.
SLOW = Drug.one_compartment(name="slow", half_life_h=30.0, ka=ka_from_tmax(1.5, 30.0), F=1.0, V_L=100.0)
# Generic two-compartment drug with well-separated rates.
TWO_COMP = Drug(name="two-comp", ka=2.0, F=0.8, V_L=20.0, k10=0.3, k12=0.6, k21=0.1)

ONE_COMP_DRUGS = [NORETHINDRONE_1C, SLOW]
ALL_DRUGS = [NORETHINDRONE, NORETHINDRONE_1C, SLOW, TWO_COMP]


def ids(d):
    return d.name


# --- The numerical solver ---------------------------------------------------

@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", ONE_COMP_DRUGS, ids=ids)
def test_single_dose_matches_bateman(drug):
    t = np.linspace(0, 3 * DAY, 2001)
    sim = simulate(drug, [0.0], 1.0, t)
    exact = bateman(drug, 1.0, t)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(sim.conc, exact, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-9 * exact.max())


@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", ONE_COMP_DRUGS, ids=ids)
def test_exact_solution_matches_bateman(drug):
    t = np.linspace(0, 3 * DAY, 501)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(exact_single_dose(drug, 1.0, t), bateman(drug, 1.0, t), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-15)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", [NORETHINDRONE, TWO_COMP], ids=ids)
def test_two_compartment_single_dose_matches_exact(drug):
    t = np.linspace(0, 3 * DAY, 2001)
    sim = simulate(drug, [0.0], 1.0, t)
    exact = exact_single_dose(drug, 1.0, t)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(sim.conc, exact, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-9 * exact.max())


@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", [NORETHINDRONE, NORETHINDRONE_1C], ids=ids)
def test_multiple_doses_match_superposition(drug):
    """Late and missed pills: the linear model's answer is a sum of single-dose curves."""
    doses = [0, 24, 51, 96, 120]  # pill 3 is 3 h late, pill 4 (72 h) skipped
    t = np.linspace(0, 7 * DAY, 3001)
    sim = simulate(drug, doses, NORETHINDRONE_DOSE_MG, t)
    exact = sum(exact_single_dose(drug, NORETHINDRONE_DOSE_MG, t - d) for d in doses)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(sim.conc, exact, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-9 * exact.max())


@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", ALL_DRUGS, ids=ids)

Levonorgestrel is metabolised in the liver to sulfate and glucuronide conjugates.

    tm,cm,auc,kt=summ(mk(ka,p)); return [np.log(cm/CMAX),np.log(tm/TMAX),np.log(auc/AUC),np.log(kt/KT)]

content.thinking: Every fit lands on the label across absorption rates of 0.4–1.2 /h, with C24 at 0.30–0.33 ng/mL and a 38% drop at 48 h. I'm fixing ka at 0.8 /h and noting that in the code before writing the fit script.

input.content:
"""Fit levonorgestrel's two-compartment parameters to Alesse day 1 (no SHBG effect).

Day 1 is a single dose, before ethinyl estradiol has raised SHBG, so it is the
only Alesse data a model without SHBG should match.

Fixed:  F = 1 (Alesse label: "bioavailability about 100%"), dose = 0.10 mg,
        ka = 0.8 /h (ASSUMED, see below).
Fitted (4 unknowns): V1, k10, k12, k21.
Targets (4, Alesse Table I, day 1):
    Cmax 2.75 ng/mL, Tmax 1.6 h, AUC 35.2 ng*h/mL,
    terminal half-life 34.3 h = ln 2 * (Vz/F) / (CL/F) = ln 2 * 2.66 / 0.0537
    (the per-kg body weight cancels, so no weight assumption is needed).

Four targets can't pin down five rates. Every ka from about 0.4 to 1.2 /h fits
all four exactly, and they all give nearly the same 24 h level and late-pill
drop; ``--profile`` prints that table. ka = 0.8 /h is a value in the middle.

Usage:  python scripts/fit_levonorgestrel.py [--profile]
Copy the printed values into src/minipill/params.py.
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import least_squares, minimize_scalar

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "src"))

from minipill.params import ALESSE_DAY1, LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG  # noqa: E402
from minipill.pk import LN2, Drug, exact_single_dose, mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml, simulate  # noqa: E402

F = 1.0
KA = 0.8
DOSE = LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG
TARGETS = {
    "cmax_ng_ml": ALESSE_DAY1["cmax_ng_ml"],
    "tmax_h": ALESSE_DAY1["tmax_h"],
    "auc_ng_h_ml": ALESSE_DAY1["auc_ng_h_ml"],
    "half_life_h": ALESSE_DAY1["half_life_h"],
}


def summarize(drug: Drug) -> dict:
    def c(t):
        return float(mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(exact_single_dose(drug, DOSE, t)))

    peak = minimize_scalar(lambda t: -c(t), bounds=(0.05, 8), method="bounded", options={"xatol": 1e-7})
    return {
        "cmax_ng_ml": -peak.fun,
        "tmax_h": peak.x,
        "auc_ng_h_ml": float(mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(drug.F * DOSE / drug.clearance_L_per_h)),  # exact AUC(0-inf)
        "half_life_h": drug.terminal_half_life_h,
    }


def make_drug(log_params, ka=KA) -> Drug:
    V, k10, k12, k21 = np.exp(log_params)
    return Drug(name="levonorgestrel", ka=ka, F=F, V_L=V, k10=k10, k12=k12, k21=k21)


def fit(ka=KA, n_starts=40, seed=0):
    def residuals(p):
        s = summarize(make_drug(p, ka))
        return [np.log(s[k] / v) for k, v in TARGETS.items()]

    best = None
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    for _ in range(n_starts):  # several starting points; keep the best fit
        x0 = np.log([25.0, 0.12, 0.3, 0.06]) + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 4)
        try:
            f = least_squares(residuals, x0, xtol=1e-14, ftol=1e-14, gtol=1e-14)
        except ValueError:  # repeated rates: exact solution undefined
            continue
        if best is None or f.cost < best.cost:
            best = f
    return make_drug(best.x, ka), best.cost


def late_pill_drop(drug: Drug) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Trough before pill 21 (on time) and the level 48 h after pill 20 (pill 21 missed)."""
    doses = np.arange(20) * 24.0
    t = np.array([20 * 24.0, 21 * 24.0])
    c = mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(simulate(drug, doses, DOSE, t).conc)
    return float(c[0]), float(c[1])


def main():
    if "--profile" in sys.argv:
        print("  ka    V1     k10    k12    k21   | C24    day-20 trough  48 h after last pill")
        for ka in (0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5):
            drug, cost = fit(ka)
            if cost > 1e-10:
                print(f"  {ka:3.1f}  no exact fit")
                continue
            c24 = float(mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(exact_single_dose(drug, DOSE, 24.0)))
            trough, late = late_pill_drop(drug)
            print(f"  {ka:3.1f}  {drug.V_L:5.1f}  {drug.k10:.3f}  {drug.k12:.3f}  {drug.k21:.3f} | {c24:.3f}  "
                  f"{trough:.3f}          {late:.3f} ({100 * (1 - late / trough):.0f}% below)")
        return

    drug, cost = fit()
    s = summarize(drug)
    print(f"Fitted parameters (ka fixed at {KA} /h, F = {F}):")
    for name in ("V_L", "k10", "k12", "k21"):
        print(f"  {name:4s} = {getattr(drug, name):.6g}")
    print(f"\nDistribution half-life (alpha): {LN2 / drug.disposition_rates[0]:.3g} h")
    print(f"Clearance: {drug.clearance_L_per_h:.2f} L/h   Vss: {drug.vss_L:.0f} L")
    print("\nTarget            label       model")
    for k, v in TARGETS.items():
        print(f"  {k:15s} {v:9.4g}   {s[k]:9.4g}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Fit levonorgestrel's two-compartment parameters to Alesse day 1 (no SHBG effect).

Day 1 is a single dose, before ethinyl estradiol has raised SHBG, so it is the
only Alesse data a model without SHBG should match.

Fixed:  F = 1 (Alesse label: "bioavailability about 100%"), dose = 0.10 mg,
        ka = 0.8 /h (ASSUMED, see below).
Fitted (4 unknowns): V1, k10, k12, k21.
Targets (4, Alesse Table I, day 1):
    Cmax 2.75 ng/mL, Tmax 1.6 h, AUC 35.2 ng*h/mL,
    terminal half-life 34.3 h = ln 2 * (Vz/F) / (CL/F) = ln 2 * 2.66 / 0.0537
    (the per-kg body weight cancels, so no weight assumption is needed).

Four targets can't pin down five rates. Every ka from about 0.4 to 1.2 /h fits
all four exactly, and they all give nearly the same 24 h level and late-pill
drop; ``--profile`` prints that table. ka = 0.8 /h is a value in the middle.

Usage:  python scripts/fit_levonorgestrel.py [--profile]
Copy the printed values into src/minipill/params.py.
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import least_squares, minimize_scalar

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "src"))

from minipill.params import ALESSE_DAY1, LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG  # noqa: E402
from minipill.pk import LN2, Drug, exact_single_dose, mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml, simulate  # noqa: E402

F = 1.0
KA = 0.8
DOSE = LEVONORGESTREL_DOSE_MG
TARGETS = {
    "cmax_ng_ml": ALESSE_DAY1["cmax_ng_ml"],
    "tmax_h": ALESSE_DAY1["tmax_h"],
    "auc_ng_h_ml": ALESSE_DAY1["auc_ng_h_ml"],
    "half_life_h": ALESSE_DAY1["half_life_h"],
}


def summarize(drug: Drug) -> dict:
    def c(t):
        return float(mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(exact_single_dose(drug, DOSE, t)))

    peak = minimize_scalar(lambda t: -c(t), bounds=(0.05, 8), method="bounded", options={"xatol": 1e-7})
    return {
        "cmax_ng_ml": -peak.fun,
        "tmax_h": peak.x,
        "auc_ng_h_ml": float(mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(drug.F * DOSE / drug.clearance_L_per_h)),  # exact AUC(0-inf)
        "half_life_h": drug.terminal_half_life_h,
    }


def make_drug(log_params, ka=KA) -> Drug:
    V, k10, k12, k21 = np.exp(log_params)
    return Drug(name="levonorgestrel", ka=ka, F=F, V_L=V, k10=k10, k12=k12, k21=k21)


def fit(ka=KA, n_starts=40, seed=0):
    def residuals(p):
        s = summarize(make_drug(p, ka))
        return [np.log(s[k] / v) for k, v in TARGETS.items()]

    best = None
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    for _ in range(n_starts):  # several starting points; keep the best fit
        x0 = np.log([25.0, 0.12, 0.3, 0.06]) + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 4)
        try:
            f = least_squares(residuals, x0, xtol=1e-14, ftol=1e-14, gtol=1e-14)
        except ValueError:  # repeated rates: exact solution undefined
            continue
        if best is None or f.cost < best.cost:
            best = f
    return make_drug(best.x, ka), best.cost


def late_pill_drop(drug: Drug) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Trough before pill 21 (on time) and the level 48 h after pill 20 (pill 21 missed)."""
    doses = np.arange(20) * 24.0
    t = np.array([20 * 24.0, 21 * 24.0])
    c = mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(simulate(drug, doses, DOSE, t).conc)
    return float(c[0]), float(c[1])


def main():
    if "--profile" in sys.argv:
        print("  ka    V1     k10    k12    k21   | C24    day-20 trough  48 h after last pill")
        for ka in (0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5):
            drug, cost = fit(ka)
            if cost > 1e-10:
                print(f"  {ka:3.1f}  no exact fit")
                continue
            c24 = float(mg_per_l_to_ng_per_ml(exact_single_dose(drug, DOSE, 24.0)))
            trough, late = late_pill_drop(drug)
            print(f"  {ka:3.1f}  {drug.V_L:5.1f}  {drug.k10:.3f}  {drug.k12:.3f}  {drug.k21:.3f} | {c24:.3f}  "
                  f"{trough:.3f}          {late:.3f} ({100 * (1 - late / trough):.0f}% below)")
        return

    drug, cost = fit()
    s = summarize(drug)
    print(f"Fitted parameters (ka fixed at {KA} /h, F = {F}):")
    for name in ("V_L", "k10", "k12", "k21"):
        print(f"  {name:4s} = {getattr(drug, name):.6g}")
    print(f"\nDistribution half-life (alpha): {LN2 / drug.disposition_rates[0]:.3g} h")
    print(f"Clearance: {drug.clearance_L_per_h:.2f} L/h   Vss: {drug.vss_L:.0f} L")
    print("\nTarget            label       model")
    for k, v in TARGETS.items():
        print(f"  {k:15s} {v:9.4g}   {s[k]:9.4g}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    doses = np.arange(0, 28 * DAY, DAY)
    t = np.linspace(0, 30 * DAY, 4001)
    sim = simulate(drug, doses, 0.35, t)
    total = sim.gut + sim.central + sim.peripheral + sim.eliminated + sim.first_pass
    np.testing.assert_allclose(total, sim.dosed, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-12)
    assert sim.dosed[-1] == pytest.approx(28 * 0.35)


def test_two_pills_at_once_is_a_double_dose():
    t = np.linspace(0, DAY, 201)
    double = simulate(NORETHINDRONE, [0, 0], 0.35, t).conc
    single = simulate(NORETHINDRONE, [0], 0.70, t).conc
    np.testing.assert_allclose(double, single, rtol=1e-10)


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "drug, expected", [(NORETHINDRONE_1C, 1.14), (SLOW, 2.35)], ids=["norethindrone-1c", "slow"]
)

    ratio = sim.conc[-1] / sim.conc[1]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("drug", [NORETHINDRONE, TWO_COMP], ids=ids)

$$\frac{dA_1}{dt} = F \, k_a \, G - (k_{10} + k_{12}) A_1 + k_{21} A_2, \qquad \frac{dA_2}{dt} = k_{12} A_1 - k_{21} A_2, \qquad C = \frac{A_1}{V_1}$$

After a dose, levels first fall quickly as drug moves into the tissues (half-life ≈ 0.8 h), then slowly as it is eliminated (half-life ≈ 7.8 h). The five rates and volume are **fitted** to the label's single-dose values (time to peak, peak, average and 24-hour levels, half-life) by `scripts/fit_norethindrone.py`, not measured. The fit can't separate absorption from the fast tissue phase, so those two rates individually aren't well determined; the curve itself is.

**Planned additions:**

- **The estrogen–SHBG effect:** ethinyl estradiol slowly raises SHBG over the cycle, and higher SHBG slows levonorgestrel clearance. The strength and speed of this effect aren't reported directly, so I calibrate them to match published data and say so clearly.

## How I know it's right

| Check | What it tests | Expected result | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exact single-dose solution | The numerical simulation | Matches the Bateman function (one compartment) and the exact matrix solution (two compartments) | ✅ Passing |
| Mass balance | No drug appears or disappears | Absorbed + eliminated + remaining = total dose | ✅ Passing |
| Steady-state accumulation | Repeated daily dosing | 1 / (1 − e^(−kτ)): ≈ 1.14 for norethindrone, ≈ 2.35 for levonorgestrel (30 h half-life) | ✅ Passing |
| Norethindrone single dose | Published label values | Peak ≈ 4,800 pg/mL near 1.2 h; ≈ 130 pg/mL at 24 h | ❌ One compartment (7.6-fold drop vs. 37-fold) · ✅ Two compartments (all label values within 5%) |
| Combined pill steady state | Published label values (0.10 mg levonorgestrel) | Steady state from day 19; peak ≈ 6.0 ng/mL, low ≈ 1.9 ng/mL | ☐ Planned |
| SHBG effect | A behavior the science requires | Without SHBG, the model underpredicts levonorgestrel's 3- to 4-fold rise; with it, the gap closes | ☐ Planned |

As expected, the one-compartment model **fails** the norethindrone 24-hour check: the measured drop is about 37-fold in 24 hours, much steeper than the 7.6-fold an 8-hour half-life predicts. A second compartment fixes it: the steep early drop is drug moving into the tissues, not leaving the body.
